title: History practice: critique an argument about 1789

messages.content:
[Session context] — picked from the learner's knowledge map when starting this session:

Propositions (id — name: statement; the problem tool's target field uses these ids):
- [n_demo_fr-mechanism] From finance to representation: Attempts to address the French monarchy's fiscal crisis brought disputes over taxation and political representation into the Estates-General.
- [n_demo_fr-multicausal] An explanation with several causes: A historical explanation of 1789 can connect fiscal crisis, institutional conflict, and popular pressures rather than treating one factor as sufficient.
- [n_demo_source-provenance] Provenance frames a source: The author, date, location, and audience of a historical document help establish the conditions in which it was produced.
- [n_demo_source-inference] Match the claim to the evidence: A document that asserts a crowd's motives directly evidences the author's assertion, but does not by itself establish every participant's motive.
- [n_demo_source-dependence] Repeated reports can share one origin: Two newspapers copying the same report are not two independent eyewitness accounts.
- [n_demo_source-bias] Bias can itself be evidence: A partisan source can provide evidence of its author's framing while requiring caution about the events or motives it describes.

messages.content: Let me practise critiquing an essay paragraph instead of memorising another list of causes.

content.text: Try this on your own. Write down your reasoning as you go.

arguments.statement: A fictional essay says: 'Two newspapers copied the same diplomatic dispatch about bread unrest, proving that every participant wanted to abolish monarchy and that hunger alone caused the Revolution.' Identify three evidential problems and propose a better argument. These invented documents are not archival quotations.
arguments.modelSolution: Copied reports are not independent corroboration. A report about unrest does not establish every participant's motive. One report cannot establish hunger as a sufficient cause of the Revolution. A stronger account identifies provenance and access, seeks independent evidence, and connects popular pressures with the fiscal crisis and disputes over taxation and representation, while qualifying motives and causal scope.

content.text: Problem posed. The learner's thinking and answer will follow.

I check independence, the size of the inference, and the causal mechanism separately. The dispatch may still show how its author framed the unrest.
